newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: South Pacific nations to cut tariffs reform economy.
newsitem.headline: South Pacific nations to cut tariffs reform economy.

text.p: Leading South Pacific nations on Friday agreed to slash tariffs, increase budget transparency and implement sweeping reforms to boost economic growth and reduce aid dependence.

Economic ministers from the 16-member South Pacific Forum agreed at their inaugural summit to adopt an action plan and work towards free trade in the region extending from Australia to the Cook Islands.
"Our goal is free and open trade and investment," the summit's host, Australian Treasurer Peter Costello, told reporters in this tropical Australian resort town.
"We believe this is concrete, specific proposals with an action plan which can continue to drive the process for economic reform in the area," Costello said.
The group includes Australia and New Zealand and 14 Pacific island nations, including Papua New Guinea and Fiji.
A joint communique outlining Friday's agreement put no timetable on implementing reforms, noting only that the pace and make-up of reforms would be "appropriate to our individual circumstances".
Costello said the lure of better economic performance and prosperity would encourage countries to meet the plan's targets.
"We don't say that it's going to be done in the immediate future, but we do say it's the aspiration of all countries over time and in accordance with their own legislative requirements," he said.
"This is a set of best practice principles which countries will be striving to meet."

The action plan reforms also include boosting private sector development, improving regulatory and transparency measures, liberalising investment policies and reducing government spending and public sectors.
The communique said members would band together to jointly argue for trade liberalisation and push the region's interests in multilateral trade groups, such as the World Trade Organisation.
The forum's two largest members, Australia and New Zealand, have economies that dwarf those of other members.
Foreign aid, particularly from Canberra, Wellington and Washington plays a key role in supporting living standards.

The remaining 14 members -- all island countries with small populations -- are the Cook Islands, Fiji, Kiribati, the Marshall Islands, the Federated States of Micronesia, Nauru, Niue, Papua New Guinea, Palau, Samoa, the Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu. The 14 island countries have economies marked by low growth, surging imports, high debt, bloated public sectors and weak private sectors, and foreign aid accounting for up to 70 percent of their gross domestic product.
Exports are largely resources, fishing rights and tourism.

Some have begun basic economic reforms, but forum leaders acknowledged at their last summit, in September, 1996, that they needed to speed the pace of change to boost their economic strength and encourage foreign investment.
